utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Would the registrar please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution, please. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. di Fazio: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I just want you to return briefly to the first weekend, so to speak, that you were in custody. You've given us details of the beatings and the conditions that you observed and of the fact that people came in, men came in and beat prisoners in the cells and outside the cells as well. Did anyone select prisoners for beating or engage in that sort of practice?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually those who came in to administer the beatings would call out people's names. They would then take these people out and beat them up. Sometimes they simply didn't like the way someone looked or they didn't like a particular reaction, and that's why they would beat such a person up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you say that people might come in to administer the beatings - sorry - that people who came in to administer the beatings would call out people's names. Can you recall any names or nicknames, any names or nicknames, of people --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who were administering the beatings or those who were being beaten? Who do you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those who were administering the beatings or calling out people's names. Any nicknames that you recall, any names.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We usually knew them by their nicknames. I don't know. Lugar, Crni, Musa, Kid. I don't know. That's as far as I can remember. Usually it was these nicknames.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do any of the defendants, to your knowledge, in this case have nicknames?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miro, Brko, Simo. I called him Simo, but he had some kind of a nickname, Solaja. As for the rest, I don't know. I don't know about Simic and the rest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Brko is the name I'm interested in. Who does that refer to?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the accused who is present here, Miroslav Tadic, nicknamed Brko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him on that weekend?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I did see him. He was moving around there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall any details of what he was up to?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he also entered the TO headquarters. Many did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. When you say "the TO headquarters" --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean the area, the area where the prisoners were, the inmates. I know that some were even suspicious, you know, and some of the local Serbs came in with some of the members of the special units; and when one of these people would say hello to one of the inmates, people thought that that was a sign, namely, that then, when the members of the special units came again, would beat up that particular person. That is the guesswork that we engaged in, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me for one moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tihic. MR. DI FAZIO: I'd like now to deal with some of the photographs, please. If Exhibit P14, all of the 71 photographs could be provided to the witness. I'll be dealing with a number of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: If we can have the use of the ELMO, Counsel, for the accused to follow? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. I agree, if Your Honours please. That's a good suggestion. Perhaps it can be switched on and we can utilise it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, would you please look at photograph number F43. There is a building depicted in that photograph. What is it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police station. Next to it is the Municipal Assembly building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. F44, what does that depict, please?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the yard of the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next one, please, F45. Is that a rear view of the police station?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour, a leading question. This is an obvious suggestion to the witness what to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, sometimes it's faster to lead where it's obvious. The witness is -- was a local resident. He knew these places. So this is not even crucial, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is just a matter of principle, Your Honour. The formulation of the question was not in accordance with the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I agree, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I agree with your approach, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Even the principles have to be approached with reason. Counsel, please continue. MR. DI FAZIO: I will attempt not to lead. I heard what Mr. Pantelic had to say yesterday. On other issues, I won't lead, but I thought that there was an indication at some stage that there wouldn't be any objection, in any event, from the Defence on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, there was that indication. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I'll press on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: F46, what buildings can you see there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first building is the building of the Municipal Assembly, and further down is again the police station. That's the smaller building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, would you also look, please, now at F50. And perhaps you could also, having looked at F50, look at F51, because I want to ask you a question about both of those photographs. F51 -- what does that -- F50, I'm sorry, F50, what does that depict?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: F50, the building of the Territorial Defence headquarters and the yard.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now, F51, what does that depict?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. It might be a view from the MUP, the police station, an office in the police station. I'm not sure, because I can't really see through the window what lies beyond. It might be an office in the police building with a view of the TO headquarters building; however, I can't see well enough, so I can't really see what you can see through the window.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look again at F46, please, and bearing -- keep handy F50 and F51. F46 depicts the -- depicts the police station and also a tree --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: F46 depicts the Municipal Assembly building and the police station, 46, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's right. Now, F46, you can see a tree in front of the police station, at least one tree. Can you comment on whether or not the tree that you can see to the left of the photograph in F50 is that tree?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you comment on whether or not the tree that you can see through the window in F51 is the same as the tree that's depicted in front of the police station in F46?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, again, we are listening to leading questions regarding the description of the tree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The location of the tree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Your colleague is still speaking. Are you still speaking? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Again, the Prosecutor is leading the witness, describing the tree in a particular way and leading the witness to say that it's one and the same tree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are speaking here about the photographs. I mean, it's just an issue of identification. I think the -- our learned friend from the Prosecutor bench should only ask the witness about the number of photographs and what is it in that particular photograph. I mean, otherwise, you know, description, tree, flower, sun, moon, others, it's not the way to deal with this. So simply -- simple facts which are the photographs, actually. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic, and the other counsel. Mr. Prosecutor, you've heard the objections, and I'm sure you will start rephrasing your questions. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I'm happy to rephrase the questions if the Chamber wishes me to do so, and of course I will do that. But none of the questions, with respect, are leading. The questions, if you look at them, are asking him to comment upon those issues. I'm not suggesting that it's the same -- suggesting it's the same tree. I'm asking him to comment upon that. Leading question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, I'm wondering, has the witness had these photographs for a while now? MR. DI FAZIO: They've certainly been shown to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Over the last few days? MR. DI FAZIO: They've been shown to him within the last few days, yes. He hasn't had them in his possession, I don't believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Now, if, you see, you have an index of photographs which describe those photographs -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Well, we would have thought that he would have gone through all the photographs, with the descriptions as shown in the index, and he could either agree or disagree, and that would really cut short; and if there's any other questions to be asked or clarification, then the clarification could be simply put to him. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Well, I haven't put the index of the photos to him and asked him to comment upon the index. I've only ever shown the photos to him and no index.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: But he has that index there on the photographs. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I don't precisely know what he's got. He may have something on the back of the photographs. If you wish me to approach the witness and see what exactly he has before him, I can do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Please go ahead. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Yes, Your Honour. He does have an index, but it's in English. I'm not aware of there ever having been a version in B/C/S, so that leads me to conclude that he's never seen an index.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Yes, but I mean, these photographs may be important, so I think perhaps by tomorrow morning you may want to get him an index in the B/C/S language. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. If the Chamber feels that it would be assisted by my doing so, of course that will be done, but what I had planned with this witness is just to go through a few photographs and get him to comment on aspects of the photographs and to identify the remainder of them through other witnesses. However, I can do that and cause an index to be created in B/C/S, and I'll make sure that it's shown to the witness. But for that to be effective, he would also have to keep and maintain with him a copy of the photographs as well; otherwise, as a tool, it won't be of any assistance to him. So I would have to do that as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to show you one other photograph. F40, please. What does that depict?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depicts the yard where the Catholic church used to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the building that you can see in the foreground?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building in the corner here is Serb Orthodox church. That's the bigger one. And the smaller building is the one where the priest lived. Because these two churches were opposite one another. Only the street divided them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you please look at F18 and F19. I hope my learned friends won't object if I lead by suggesting that you can see some green space there. Is that green space that you see there with grass in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's in Bosanski Samac. It's the area where the mosque used to be, Aziza. A bit further off you can see the department store, et cetera. The mosque is no longer there, but that's where it used to be.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And finally, would you look at photographs F36 and F37, please. What do they show?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These buildings are owned by my brother and myself. This is where my law office was. It still says "law office" here. Then this is where the shop was, and this is where the restaurant was. MR. DI FAZIO: I've finished with the photographs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday I was asking you some questions about events after the weekend, and you described a meeting that you had. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the evening, Monday, we talked, Simo Zaric, Stevan Todorovic and I, if that's the meeting you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. You told us that you had asked to be released, pleaded to be released, and that those pleas were uttered when either Simo Zaric or the other gentleman, Mr. Sarkanovic, was present.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you provided with any hope of release?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the day, they did give me hope that I would be released. However, after this conversation that took place afterwards in the evening with Blagoje Simic or, rather, especially with Todorovic, then I was not really given any hope. They took me down to the cells, downstairs; that, I already referred to. Truth to tell, there was from time to time some hope that one could get out, but that seemed quite distant. There weren't any more promises, like the ones they gave during the first two or three days, that we would be released.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Following your return to the cells, from that point on, did you ever see Lugar again?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe that was the next day; so it was on a Tuesday. Allegedly a man from Slatina got killed, and he went to his funeral. And then after the funeral, he came to us, to that area where we were, and he told us, "I swore on the grave that I will have my revenge." I think the name of the person who was killed was Luka. He was killed in a conflict with the HVO. And he looked at me at the end and he said, "You will be the last." And then he beat each person one by one, and then he took me out and he hit me with his knuckles, with his fist. And I didn't know that the blow could throw you back several metres. And then, after each blow, he would hit me, he would kick me. And then after a while, when I couldn't get up anymore, he jumped on my chest. I placed my arms in this position, and I could hear cracking, something cracking. Then he picked me up. I had a Tissot watch. It was a thicker watch. And he took this watch and he hit me on the head with that watch several times, so that there was blood coming from the place where he hit me. I also had blood coming out of my mouth. He also had some bombs on his belt. He was fully armed. And then he was not sure whether he wanted to kill me or not. And then at the end he just pushed me away. He said, "Get away," and then he pushed me back into the cell. That happened the first time, when I was at the police station, when I was beaten. After that, they called us out to eat. Yesterday I mentioned Hranaprodukt, but actually it was Utva where they took us so that everybody could see that I was all bloody; all the inmates as well as the people who were guarding us. And that's when they took us to lunch.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What exactly is Utva --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, counsel for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, pardon me, my legal objection is non-responsive. The witness's answer was not responsive to the question. This is very, very important information we are receiving from the witness right now. The question presented from the Prosecutor was: "Did you ever see Lugar again?" And it's important that we proceed in question and answer so that we can make any objections if we need to. So my specific objection is non-responsive. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I didn't appreciate very much the object of the objection, but I'm sure counsel understood it and will insist on questions being answered by the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. With respect to my learned friend, I don't see that this gives rise to an objection. If I ask a witness a question and he doesn't give what in Defence counsel's view is a relevant answer, well, that's just a matter of -- that's just nothing that, A, I can do it and, B --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because counsel can cross-examine afterwards. MR. DI FAZIO: Exactly. Exactly. And without going into the transcript and analysing it right now, with respect to my learned friend, the answers aren't what one would call blatantly irrelevant, so I haven't got any problems with the evidence I'm eliciting with the witness, so I'm not concerned with his answers. I'll make that plain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in addition to what my learned colleague just said, I would like to reiterate another point. Now, witness is going to adjust his previous statement from yesterday about the name, description, et cetera. I think that it cannot be done now. I mean, what was said, it was said. Now, we are heading to the other direction, to the other events and other things. Otherwise, each day, after previous day of statement, each witness can adjust or prepare or clarify, et cetera. It is not the aim and it is not the spirit of the examination-in-chief, and his testimony. Thank you so much. I mean, "I recall better today than yesterday." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: But, counsel, those are matters for credibility, and you can take them up on cross-examination and in your submissions, if a witness keeps changing his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: That's fodder for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. That's right. But acting in capacity of the officer of justice here, I must reiterate these things; that we are to some extent we are wasting time, Your Honours, because we are here three or four days now, we are at the level of the local events in Bosanski Samac, and now we are speaking about what was the restaurant, what was the name, et cetera. That's my impression. Okay, of course, we are free in cross-examination to point out all these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. The more objections you take on matters which you can raise in cross-examination, the more time we shall waste. And I'm sure you are aware of the reasons why we can't sit afternoons as well. I'm sure that has been explained to you, and I don't think it's a matter that you should take up at this time of examination-in-chief of this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are going through with difficulties in this trial which are appreciated by everybody, and the less objections which are not really reasonable, the better. Counsel, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you so much. MR. DI FAZIO: I don't want to answer what my learned friend says, but the witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You don't need to answer. Just go ahead. MR. DI FAZIO: Where was I?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was a simple one: What is Utva?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Utva is a factory in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever leave the custody of the police in the -- or custody and the police station any time up to the point of -- at which you were taken to Brcko, in the period of time leading up to the transfer?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't leave. I was taken home to be searched. But even then I was accompanied by police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe the circumstances of this episode to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of those -- of the special forces came up to me and he said -- asked me if I had any money. I had 500 marks, German marks, in my wallet. And because that wasn't enough for him, he asked me did I have any money at home? And I said that I did. And then he, with another colleague, took me out, put me in a car, and first we stopped off at the offices of the Party of Democratic Action. They searched the premises. He collected some papers there. Then we came in front of my house. His colleague wanted to fire, shoot, at the house, with a rocket launcher, zolja, but the other guy told him not to do that. Then we went inside the house. The house had been broken into. In the living-room, the video was missing. We went to the bedroom where I kept my money, and in a -- in a side table, we found 2.000 German marks. He pointed a gun at my forehead and he said, "Do you have any more?" On the other side of the bedside cabinet, there was more money, and we took that out. Then he pointed the rifle at me again and asked me, "Is there any more?" So that in two more places in the room, I took the money where I used to hide that money. So I gave him money from two other places. There was some shillings, German marks, francs. It was about 5.500 to 6.000 German marks. On that occasion, he found my hunting rifle, and he also took that rifle. Then he took me -- took me back to the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The men who accompanied you, how were they dressed? I'm really interested in whether or not they were military men and, if so, what type of military men.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were in camouflage uniforms. They were special forces from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What makes you say they were from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could tell by the way they spoke. You noticed that right away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In the days following this episode, were you taken out of your cell for any reason?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was taken out on two occasions: When I was beaten; I was also taken out for interrogation, interrogation that was at my request. I asked to be interrogated once.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned two occasions when you were taken out for beating. Can you please describe those occasions, preferably in sequence, to the Court.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time, a member of the special forces in camouflage uniform from Serbia came to get me. He was missing an index finger. He took me upstairs to the office of the criminal investigations unit. I know that this man was drinking whiskey. And he asked me to make a list of the Muslims who had weapons. I was trying to remember, but I couldn't. But this didn't seem to matter to him. He beat me. He kept hitting me over and over. And at one point, he opened the door and he kept hitting me. I was going, walking through the hall, and I was going to the end of the hall, and he kept hitting me. At that moment, while he was hitting me, Simo Zaric and the late Milos Bogdanovic were coming towards me. There were also -- there was also another man with them, Bokan. He was from Serbia. I think Marko Tuvakovic was there as well. And this person Bokan said, "Why are you hitting him? Just kill him." And he took out a pistol from his pocket. It was a white, nickel pistol, and he placed it at my temple, and it clicked. And Bokan said, "What is this? There's something wrong." And then he pulled the trigger again and nothing happened once more. And then he pushed me away and he said, "Well, just go on," as if to tell this person to continue to beat me. That was one occasion when I was beaten.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't want to leave that episode yet. You mentioned a hall. Can you recall which floor of the police station this hall was in?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the first floor of the police station.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were being struck by the man -- I withdraw that. When you were being threatened with the pistol by the man called Bokan, where was Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was standing right there. All of the people that I mentioned were standing there. They came out of that office together, the office where Simo worked, and that's how we met.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say anything to any of these men at the time that the gun was being held to you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. This happened very quickly. I was just thinking whether this pistol would go off. I think that I didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you describe the next episode when you were taken out of the cells?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second time was maybe the next day, at some time in the evening, around 11.00 or 12.00 at night. Two people came. I know that one of them was called Musa, and I think the other person who was there was the man with the missing index finger who took me out the day before. And they hit me once or twice in the cell, and they called me out, as well as a reserve police officer from the village of Hasici, and they took us upstairs again to the office of the criminal investigations unit chief where I was beaten the day before. It was dark inside. And first of all they hit this police officer from Hasici with a baton about ten times, and then they continued to beat me. One of them was holding a lamp. You couldn't see them; you could just see this light. And if you'd turn, as you turned towards the lamp, you would receive a blow to one side and then to the other side. One of them put the barrel of a pistol into our mouth. They were asking for money, but we didn't have any money. And they were saying, "What about friends who can give money for you?" This beating went on for at least an hour, and they were telling us, "Lie down like this," and they would beat us. Then we would have to stretch our arms out, and they would hit us with the baton on our arms, with a truncheon. Then they took us back to the ground floor. It was already -- there was light there, light coming in from the street, and they continued to hit us. At one point they brought in a jar of hot peppers, chilli peppers, and they told us, "Eat the peppers." A few days before, we didn't receive very much food, so I took one of those chilli peppers and ate it. They hit us. They cursed us. Then they took a handful of those chilli peppers and forced them into our mouth, and they kept hitting us. I fell onto a table that was there. Then they kept asking for the names of people who can give money for me. While I was in that room, they were beating us. Then they would go across the street to the headquarters of the TO, and then they would come back, and then they would hit us some more. At that time it was already 1.00 or 2.00 a.m. Simo Zaric came by with Toso, and he could see the condition that I was in. I asked him, "Please, if you can help me at all." And Simo said, "No. No, I can't. Things are the way they are," and he just shrugged. After that they wanted to take me out to execute me. They said, "Let's go and execute him now." They took me down the hall. The other person was saying, "Oh, just leave him. We will hang him tomorrow at 11.00. This has been agreed. We'll take him out to the centre of town, and we'll hang him there." And then they kept hitting me all the way until we reached the cell at the end of the corridor, and this lasted from 11.00 at night until 3.00 in the morning. I was covered with blood. Well, the next day is another story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get on to the next day in just a moment. Who is the man Toso? I'm sorry if I don't have the pronunciation correct.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Toso, Tutnjevic. He came with Simo Zaric. He was a driver in the Municipal Committee. He was my neighbour. He lived close to me. They were in Brcko that night, so on the way back they stopped there. That's what I heard them saying while we were all in the hall, in the corridor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is Mr. Tutnjevic's ethnic background, please?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tutnjevic, Toso, is a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You say that they were in Brcko that night and on the way back they stopped at the police station. How do you know that they were in Brcko that night and that they stopped at the police station?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the basement. When you come into the SUP, to the right of the duty officer's room, and there was a door there that was open. These two men were beating me. They would then go out and go to the TO headquarters. And they kept the door open, so that I could hear when Simo came. I could hear him saying that he was in Brcko, that there was a corridor established there which will never be cut off again. And I had never heard Simo talk about Serbs and Serbian matters so much. He before would always be talking about Yugoslav things. Now he was talking about what the Serbs did, their links with Yugoslavia. He didn't see me, because I was up there in the office. And I know on that occasion, he was telling those men -- and also when he came in to see me, I know that he was in the barracks in Brcko. He had just come back from that trip, and Tutnjevic was the person who was driving him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recall with any more detail his comments about the establishment of the corridor?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult to remember all of that right now, but I know that he said the Serbs have now established a corridor that will never be cut off. They will never allow it to be cut off, the corridor linking the Serb areas here, Krajina and so on, with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Eventually the beating must have finished. Were you taken back to your cells?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was taken back to the cell. This was perhaps at 3.00 a.m. And I just kept thinking when they were going to come and get me the next day to hang me. In the morning, I asked for Simo to see me, to talk to him, to try to get him to save me from being hanged.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you go about trying to get to see him? What actions did you take?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported to the duty officer and asked for Simo to see me, to talk to him. The duty officer conveyed this. And then after a while, perhaps after about an hour, Simo called me to come upstairs to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the duty officer and where was the duty officer to be found?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a guard in front of the door. It wasn't a police duty officer. We would tell him what we needed, and then he would convey it. I don't remember his name. I think that he was from Obudovac. It's a village near Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken to Mr. Zaric's office?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they took me to the office. I sat down in his office. We talked about the events of the night before, the beating. He was against that as well. He said -- if I can talk about what happened next, but I don't want to exceed the limits of the question. I know that when they said that they would come and get me at 11.00, I was in that office and I could see Lugar coming in a yellow Golf vehicle and I could see him speeding. And then about 30 metres before the police station, he started braking, and he was braking so hard that everyone in the police station could hear the sound of that braking. He stopped in front of the police station. I saw him enter the police station. And then I heard from the others that he went inside and he asked for me. And when he didn't find me in the cell, he crossed over to the TO headquarters. Then he killed a Croat from Slavonja whose name was Dikan, and we heard that shot upstairs. And then Simo asked the duty officer to make a report about what happened, and the officer on duty that said Lugar had killed this man Dikan. And Simo started cursing. He called Blagoje Simic, and I know that he got him on the line, and he said, "That fool killed a man." I don't know what Blagoje's response was, but I could see Simo then saying, "Well, 50 people saw it." So I concluded then that Blagoje had asked whether anyone had seen it. And then he asked where Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic was, and Blagoje said that he was around. They were in Utva, on some kind of visit to Samac, and that then he was going to see Blagoje, as the president of the municipality, and they were going to go to lunch. And then Simo said that he wanted to see the lieutenant colonel, and he called for Miroslav Tadic to come, who was sort of -- who was his assistant, some kind of a person who usually accompanied him. And then Miroslav Tadic came and they went to Utva, I think, in a car to talk to Nikolic. Afterwards, Simo came and said, "The army will come to take you out of Samac." We didn't know where we would be taken or how. Then they took me to a different room upstairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, if I can ask you to pause there. Do you know a gentleman named Ibrahim Salkic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know the man. I know a man named Ibrahim Salkic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in custody?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was in custody at the TO headquarters together with me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he in custody on the day of this episode that you have just described where Dikan was killed?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before Dikan was killed, Lugar took Salkic to the TO headquarters courtyard and beat him there. And we saw him. Simo and I saw that. We saw him beating him. And we see him jumping up from these blows and moaning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just slow it down. I want to ask you a few more detailed questions about this. Is it -- as I read your evidence, is it your position that this beating of Mr. Salkic took place at around the same time as this -- the killing of Dikan?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it precede it, or did it follow it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Salkic was beaten by him first and that then he killed the other man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when you saw Salkic being beaten?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Simo's office, and you can see the yard of the TO headquarters quite well from the window there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described him - I should say Lugar - arriving with a squeal of wheels.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Presumably, the beating of Salkic followed upon that. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, soon after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you seated when you saw this, or were you standing at the window?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was standing by the window, because I was watching him through the window, expecting him to come up to me. I was afraid that they would come up to Simo and ask for me so that they could beat me too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Where was Simo Zaric when you were standing at the window?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in that office. I think that at one moment, he stood there watching what was going on too, Salkic's beating. He saw that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just pause for a moment, think back. At the time that were you standing at the window looking at the events that you could see in the courtyard, tell the Chamber what you looked like. I want the Chamber to get an idea of what appearance you had.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said that I had been beaten the previous night. I probably washed my face, washed the blood off in the morning. I must have looked exhausted, tired, perhaps with some bruises. I don't know. But I think that the blood had been removed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you changed your clothes at all?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There was no possibility for me to change. I always wore the same clothes. From the moment I got into the camp until the moment I left, I always wore the same clothes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's get back to the events that you observed. How long did the beating of Salkic last?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps about 15 minutes, 20, something like that. It seems to me that Lugar beat him with some kind of a stick, about a metre long. It was not a police truncheon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you comment on what was going on, or did Simo Zaric comment on what was going on?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Of course I was protesting there, and Simo was also condemning the fact that this was taking place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The beating finished. What did Lugar do?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lugar then walked in, I guess. That's what the other inmates told me. Of course, I only heard the gunshot. However, from the others who were present there, I heard that on the previous day he had beaten that man Dikan and that Dikan lay there unconscious. And this time, when Lugar came, he put his ear down by his head to see whether he was still breathing, and then when he realised that he still was breathing, then he took his pistol out and shot him. That's what the other people had told me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was this man, Dikan? Did you know him?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know him. Perhaps by sight. They say that he is from Slavonski Samac, that he often came to Samac, and that people knew him. He liked to be in -- he liked to hang around in restaurants and cafes. And that evening he was in a restaurant that had been raided and all the Muslims were taken in, and since he was a Croat, he was taken in too. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me? I just want to look at a previous portion of the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, your original objective in -- as I understand your evidence, was to get out of the cell and avoid being hung. That was your fear, as I understand your evidence.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I got there, I told Simo what they had told me, that they wanted to hang me. And that's why I went up to see him. I felt safer there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he provide any solace?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he said that he would do his best, that he would take all measures to get us out of this camp. He saw what the situation was. He saw how we were all beaten up. And he promised that he would do that through the JNA. And that's what he did. In the afternoon, a captain named Petrovic came - and I know that with Simo and Stevan Todorovic, and I don't know who else - he made a list of persons who would be taken away from there. This took a long time. I know that this went into the night. And one moment towards the end, Simo came to see me. I was in a room over there in the dark, and he said, "I did it. You're on this list too. You'll get out of the camp. You're going with the military." And he expressed his pleasure over the fact that things were that way. He hugged me. He kissed me. Perhaps about ten minutes later, Stiv also came and he said that he was giving me yet another chance, "You'll get out now." He said, "You're going with the military." But he was putting it as if it were his merit. But I knew that it had not been his doing, but let it be. Then trucks came. But all this time those members of the special units were no longer there. When there was the first talk concerning our departure to Brcko, ever since the killing of this Dikan, they were not there. At least I didn't hear that they were at the police station. And then they called out our names and surnames. We got onto these trucks. At any rate, we all got into the trucks, and perhaps six or seven of them had stayed back. I think that Izet Izetbegovic was among them. He stayed there. And also Luka Gregurevic, a policeman who is deceased now, he was there too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask you just to pause there. You say that -- earlier in this answer, you told the Chamber that Simo Zaric and Stevan Todorovic and possibly someone else made a list of persons who would be taken away. How do you know that they made such a list? Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Opposite the office where I was detained, there was an office where Mihajlo Topolovac, the former commander, worked, and it was he who dictated this list. And I saw when people came to see him. And he would also go to this other room where Todorovic and Simo Zaric were, and also this Petrovic. So Simo and Todorovic came to see me. And I realised on the basis of what they said, they were the ones who were making these lists. They made these lists and they said, "You'll get out, and the JNA will take you," things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you have an opportunity to see the former commander who dictated the list at work, preparing that list? When did you have an opportunity to see that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The former commander of the police station, Mihajlo Topolovac, I saw him because he -- I was in the office opposite his, and the two of us knew each other personally, in every possible way. And I went there to see Topolovac, and he said, "Do not spend much time here. Go elsewhere. Somebody might see you here." And I think that he also asked me about something because they were taking down people's details and whatever. So I think he asked me about some of my personal details.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've described an episode where you were in Mr. Zaric's office and you saw Ibrahim Salkic beaten and you heard the gunshot in which Dikan was killed. What I want to know, was it on this occasion that you spoke -- you saw Topolovic [sic], or was it on another occasion? That's all I want to know.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Topolovac. Topolovac; I saw him. I saw him in the afternoon that day; that is to say, after the killing, after the beating. Perhaps he had been in the building, but that's when I first saw him. I first saw him in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. How long were you in the office of Mr. Zaric, or at least in the police station, on this occasion when you -- when Dikan was killed? Was it a whole afternoon, a matter of half an hour, an hour? Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Simo's office perhaps in the morning at 10.00 and then until the moment when Simo went to talk to Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic. Perhaps it was until 2.00. I don't know. Until 2.00 in the afternoon, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it during this period of time that you saw Topolovac engaged in his work?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I was in the office. I didn't go out anywhere. I can't remember. But what I do know is that he was there in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken back to the cells before you were loaded onto the truck?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Directly from the upstairs floor where I had been, I was taken to the truck, because they were calling out people's names. They called out my name, and then I left. I did not go back to the cell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were people being put onto the truck from both the police station and from the TO? Were they assembling towards the truck from those two locations?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They were brought in a line, and the people were brought from the TO. Then their names were being called out, and they boarded the truck one by one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you guarded?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where I was that day in the afternoon, there was a young man in the hallway. But it's not that he was guarding me, particularly. I think his name was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, Mr. Tihic. I meant when you were on the truck and being transported to Brcko. I'm now concentrating on that.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That was the army that took over, and they transported us. The military police was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long does it take to get to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Brcko is about 55 kilometres away from Samac. Perhaps we travelled for about an hour by this truck, perhaps a bit more. And we didn't know where we were going then, and later on we saw that this was the JNA barracks at Brcko. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I want to at this point ask Mr. Tihic to point out the location of Brcko, and to do so I would like to use the large Times map of the former Yugoslavia. Perhaps that could be placed on the easel. I've got copies in black and white of this particular map. I'm sure it's a map that would be familiar to many people in the courtroom. I'm going to seek to tender the large map that we see on the easel into evidence, and I'd ask that it be provided with an exhibit number. And I can also provide the copies if the Chamber feels that it's appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. What is the title of the map? What is the map called? MR. DI FAZIO: The title, for the purposes of the exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The proceedings, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: -- and the proceedings will be "The Times map of the Balkans." Is that sufficient for descriptive purposes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Can we have the number, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Times map of the Balkans shall be marked for the record as Prosecutor Exhibit P15. MR. DI FAZIO: It's big. Unfortunately, it's not quite as big as I hoped, but I'll have copies there. In fact, perhaps I might also refer to Exhibit P12, which is a small map of the area around Bosanski Samac, Exhibit P12, and that would be better suited for use on the ELMO, which might actually be better than The Times map which I've just tendered into evidence. So perhaps if P12 could be provided. I have a copy here which can be placed upon the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just point out for the benefit of the Court where Brcko appears.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How long did this trip take to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps an hour, an hour or so. It's about 55 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many trucks? Was it just one, or were there more?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken to in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took us to the JNA barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where is that in Brcko? Is that in the central part of the town? Is it on the outskirts of the town? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's on the outskirts of town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Dragan Lukac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [redacted] He was all bruised, all over his legs, his body, his head. I think that he was beaten more than anybody else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just tell the Court how long you remained in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We remained in Brcko perhaps for about five or six days, something like that, and they didn't beat us there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll get on to events in Brcko in just a moment. Where were you taken from Brcko?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Brcko, they took us to the JNA barracks in Bijeljina on the 1st of May, when the bridge was destroyed. The name of the barracks is Fadil Jahic Spanac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. -- I see Mr. Pantelic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I think that the witness said that Brcko, town Brcko, was attacked, and I cannot see on the transcript this expression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps the Prosecutor can clear that with the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, you heard the issue raised by Mr. Pantelic. Did you in fact mention anything about an attack on Brcko?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 1st of May, the Yugoslav People's Army attacked Brcko and the other units. And on that day, because of that state of war in Brcko, they transferred us to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us now of the conditions that existed at Brcko, the conditions under which you were incarcerated?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we arrived in Brcko, there was a regular procedure involved. The military policemen frisked us. Then they put us into the cells of the military prison. There were iron bars on these cells. Three or four of us, [redacted], were put in a room separate from the other detainees. They handcuffed us, and we were some kind of extremists. And then they kept us there for one night and we had to sleep with handcuffs on. The next day they transferred us, together with the other prisoners, to these cells. Nobody beat us there in Brcko. The military policemen were saying that they were ready to beat us, they had prepared themselves for that, but when they saw what we looked like, they felt sorry for us and they didn't beat us. There was food. They brought it. And also there was a doctor who came and examined people, things like that, because a lot of people had been hurt and these wounds had to be healed in a way, things like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to observe military men either guarding you or in and around the barracks?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Inside we were guarded by soldiers of the JNA. That was the military police. The Red Berets came up too. I know they would come to the door and then they would swear at us, saying that they would slaughter us, things like that. I also saw them in the barracks. But these policemen did not let them beat us. The military policemen did not let them beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just explain to the Chamber who you understood the Red Berets to be and why you had that understanding.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my understanding was then that these were some special units that in a way are part of the army but, on the other hand, have their own freedom to act. For dirty jobs, so to speak, that's what they were used for: when a certain area had to be mopped up, when people were supposed to be intimidated, things like that. Since ordinary soldiers could not do that, they could not simply kill people, rape them, et cetera. Then they would rush in, do it for them, and then the army would move in to an area that had already been taken care of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did these Red Berets have any apparent leader?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not notice that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We have to take our break, Counsel. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. There is just a matter -- that's an appropriate point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You can answer. MR. DI FAZIO: But there is a matter that I want to raise just briefly with Your Honours before we break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: There was an objection earlier, and I didn't raise it at that point because I think Your Honour was keen for me to press on. There was an objection earlier to this witness changing something, a portion of his evidence, the name of a factory, and I didn't say anything about that. I think the witness might have had an opportunity of hearing that. In my submission, the witness is not only permitted to change his evidence if he wishes to do so but is also obliged to do so, because he's duty-bound to try to provide to the Court as many details, as many honest details, as he can. If his memory tells him that he gave some misleading evidence to the Chamber yesterday, then he is to be commended and encouraged to come along the following day and to set matters right with the Tribunal, and I don't want him to be inhibited or feel that he shouldn't be able to do so. And so that's what I wanted to raise with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, that is the correct approach. So we shall take our break and resume at 11.30 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, the Prosecution is continuing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, just before we start, I don't believe we have the witness's date of birth. Could we have that, please? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, can you provide the Chamber with your date of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: November 26th, 1951, in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm still dealing now with the period of time at which you were at Brcko. During that time, did you see any of the defendants?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Simo Zaric for sure. As for the rest, I don't know. I saw Simo Zaric for sure, but I'm not certain about the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Under what circumstances did you see Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo came with Captain Petrovic. I think Lazar Stanisic was with them, also Fadil Topcagic. I remember that they talked to us through the door. And I know that Petrovic told to me -- told me about the barricades that were put up and said that I had organised that, and I told him that I did not. And he said, "Okay. Simo believes that you didn't do it, so let's leave it at that." That time, when they came, I don't remember exactly who it was or whether it was Lazar Stanisic or Fadil said that we should be released around the 1st of May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Earlier this week, I believe, you gave evidence about an episode involving barricades in Bosanski Samac. Did you understand this reference by Fadil Topcagic to be a reference to that episode that you described earlier in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fadil Topcagic talked at the TO headquarters for the first time about the possibility of our being -- of us being released. The second time, Fadil talked about the possibility of our release on May 1st at the barracks in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until this point, had you been informed by anyone -- I'm not talking about what you concluded from interrogations, but had you been informed, told, by anyone why you were being kept in custody?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were never specifically charged with anything. We never received any kind of detention order. On one occasion, at the barracks in Brcko, Simo did say that several of us were political prisoners. He mentioned me and Kadic [phoen], Franjo, and another person. And he said this not as if we were going to receive any kind of order about that, but he just said that during a conversation, that five or six of us were political prisoners and the others were just regular; probably meaning that they were less responsible or not responsible at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I see counsel, Defence counsel, on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have objection to the transcript. As far as I remember, the witness said the name Lukac, and I don't see his name in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps counsel can correct that with the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I'm grateful to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Earlier when you were describing the -- who Simo Zaric identified as political prisoners, you mentioned some names. Did you also mention the name of Lukac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the name of Dragan Lukac.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you identify the occasion when Simo Zaric mentioned this issue of your status as political prisoners? Was it during an interrogation? Was it an offhand remark in your cell? Can you give us more details of this occasion?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened in the JNA barracks in Brcko, because Simo, Petrovic -- Captain Petrovic, Stanisic, and Topcagic were on one side of the prisoner bars and we were on the other side. And there was talk about us being released on May 1st, even on the day itself, May 1st, and Simo mentioned this to all of us. He said that several of us were political prisoners at Brcko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever seek details as to -- let me phrase my question, please. Did you ever seek details as to what aspect of your political views or political activities had caused you to acquire this status of political prisoner?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't ask, and I didn't have the opportunity to ask something like that. I don't know whether Simo came again after that. And also, that was probably one of the reasons why I never asked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it your position, then, that you saw Mr. Zaric only on one occasion at Brcko, or were there more occasions, other than this episode when you were spoken to through the bars and your status as political prisoner was raised?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that he came once. It's possible that he came again, but I'm sure about this one time that he came.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think earlier you said that you were eventually taken to Bijeljina. Before you were taken to Bijeljina, before, were you removed at any time from those barracks?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At one time we were called by the prison warden. He was a captain. He was bald. His hand was in a plaster cast. He was injured. He said that several of us had to go to Bosanski Samac to give a statement for television. And shortly after that, they got us ready, myself and Safet Hadzialijagic, Omer Nalic. We sat in the pinzgauer vehicle, and they took us to Bosanski Samac, and Izet Izetbegovic was waiting for us there. They also wanted him to appear in that television programme.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken first when you arrived in the town of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First they took us to Omer Nalic's house, where his wife was, and we had a bath there. They told us to have a bath. And Fadil Topcagic --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just pause there. How long had it been since you had had a bath?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the 18th. And let's say this was the 29th. I'm not sure exactly what date it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What clothes were you wearing? I mean by that, when you were en route to Bosanski Samac, what were you wearing?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was wearing the clothes that I was detained in. And then when we came to Samac, we stopped in front of the SUP building, and Fadil Topcagic took a van or a car and they took us to the apartment, to the flat of Omer Nalic, where we had a bath. His wife was there. She was crying. She was looking at us when we took our clothes off. We were full of bruises. After that, Fadil drove me to my house, where I found another suit, and I put it on so that I would look better and neater on television.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whose idea was it that you put on a suit in order to look neater and better? Was it your idea or was it someone else's?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me that I needed to go home and change. The clothes that I was wearing were creased, blood-stained, and I wanted to change anyway. I didn't feel comfortable wearing the same clothes for 10 or 12 days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You cleaned up, changed clothes. Then what happened?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then they took us back to the police station again. I know that I was in one office first with Vlado Sarkanovic. Simo Krunic was there. I know him from my street. And we were waiting for them to call us out for the taping. Fadil even brought something for us to eat. They were saying that this should stop now, that things would be better. They introduced a note of optimism.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fadil who?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fadil Topcagic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you eventually interviewed?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An interview was taped in the office where Simo Zaric worked. That's where it took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was present?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a journalist from TV Novi Sad. I found out Simo was there, Simo Zaric, who was asking the questions. Stevan Todorovic was there. At one point, Crni came in and said that they should bring me downstairs after the taping because he wanted to talk to me, so that I could tell him something about the shelling of Slavonia and Samac. So the interview was taped. There were questions. I know that when the interview was finished, when Simo finished with his questions, Stevan Todorovic asked that I say that we were not beaten by the Serb police. So the journalist put that question to me later, and I said that they did not beat us, because I wasn't in a position to --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to pause there? First of all, where is Novi Sad?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Novi Sad is in Yugoslavia, in Voyvodina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just point it out to the Chamber? Could you just stand up and point it out on the Times map, the location of Novi Sad? Is it in the --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters cannot hear the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: I think the Chamber saw where the location of the town is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's in Serbia, in the Autonomous Province of Voyvodina, which is in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I need some other details. You say that Todorovic asked that you say that you were not beaten by Serb police. When he asked that, where was Simo Zaric?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the same room, and, you know, I stated that I wasn't beaten by the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When Crni came in and asked that they should take you downstairs because he wanted to talk to you, do you know if Simo Zaric was present?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simo was sitting there. He just opened the door and maybe just stepped inside the room. He didn't come into the room. And he said loudly that they needed to bring me downstairs so that I could name some names of Muslims who are allegedly providing the coordinates to the Croats to fire at the agricultural estate. And I said that I -- "I don't know anybody." And he said, "Well, you'll come downstairs."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you feel about that, being told that Crni wanted to speak to you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I was frightened because I knew what that meant, what it meant to go downstairs, to him and his -- I mean, there was no question of that being a conversation. It was being beaten up. There was no conversation. So that during the whole of the interview, I was afraid because I had to go downstairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Simo Zaric present throughout the interview?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he participate in it? By that, I mean asking questions.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an anchor, let's say, of that programme. I think he was wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any ammunition or weapons or bombs or anything like that on display in the room?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've, I think, mentioned earlier in your evidence a gentleman named Lieutenant Colonel Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I mentioned him several times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see him during the day that you were interviewed, on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see any other prisoners who apparently participated in interview -- in the interview?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw the people that I mentioned who came with me from Brcko. And I also saw Izet Izetbegovic, who stayed in Samac when we were taken to Brcko. And I saw Toto [Realtime transcript read in error "Todorovic"] Ramusovic called Nizan, and I saw that he also gave a statement. But he wasn't an inmate. He was a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, we have a transcript objection. Here it said "Todorovic," and this would probably indicate Stevan Todorovic, but I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Which line?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one second. It's line 21. And I believe that the witness was speaking about the nickname Toto.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps Prosecution counsel can clear that with the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Todorovic in reference to a gentleman named Ramusovic. First of all, was that Stevan Todorovic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said -- when I mentioned Nizan Ramusovic, called Toto, I meant by that name the person that I saw in the corridor of the police station. That person wasn't in the office where the taping was being done. Stevan Todorovic, on the other hand, was the chief of police, who was in the office at the time of the taping. They are two different persons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to show you now a video. MR. DI FAZIO: For the benefit of the Defence, they will -- they will know this video as V1 on the list of exhibits, entitled, "Genocide in Bosanski Samac," and I can provide -- indeed, I think transcripts have been provided to the Chamber and to Defence counsel. If Your Honours please, may I just tell you how I propose to deal with this evidence? It's a longish interview and depicts a number of people. I don't propose to play it all from beginning to end now but rather to fast-forward my way through it until I get to points at which I wish to stop and ask the witness questions about that. I do so because, A, we will have the transcript and we can look at the transcript and gather what we need from that transcript and make submissions on it at a later stage, if necessary, and, B, because of the time constraints, I want to get the matter moving as quickly as I can. Unless there is objections, I indicate that that's what I will proceed to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I see no objections. Can we have the number for the footage and the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may just ask: Should separate numbers be given to the transcript and the videotape, or are they one exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: One and then slash, whether it's ter or /1, /A. That's up to you. You use your system.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The videotape shall be marked for the record as Prosecutor's Exhibit P16, and the transcript shall be - which I believe is English - shall be marked for the record as P16A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And the Serbo-Croat transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The Serbo-Croat transcript shall be marked for the record as P16A ter. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours just bear with me. I want to ask a question of my colleague.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tihic, I want to show you excerpts from this particular video. MR. DI FAZIO: And I would ask that the gentleman in the technical room now play it at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see that gentleman displayed on the screen now, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do see him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Lieutenant Colonel Stefan Nikolic. It says so here too, but even without that, I would have recognised him. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Please fast-forward again.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Pause there, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise any of those women? If you don't, just say so.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are women from Samac. I know them by sight. I think that this one is Gordana.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which one? The one on the left or the one on the right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my left-hand side. Gordana, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know their ethnic backgrounds? If you don't know, just say so.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Gordana can be either a Serb or a Croat. I'm not sure. And I think the one next to her is a Muslim, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are they Bosanski Samac residents? Perhaps I should ask: Were they Bosanski Samac residents back in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Please fast-forward.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the gentleman on the right?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On my right, you mean? On my right-hand side is the journalist, and on the left-hand side is Simo Zaric. So the journalist is on the right and Simo Zaric is on the left, from my point of view. That's the white ribbon I was telling you about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. MR. DI FAZIO: Could we now just progress at normal speed for a while, with volume.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the interpreters please have a reference to the transcript page. MR. DI FAZIO: Perhaps if it could be stopped there. I don't intend to play it at this stage. Finding it on the transcript at this point would be rather difficult.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The gentleman apparently holding the microphone is, or appears to be, an interviewer. Can you say if he's the man who interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, this is a journalist from TV Novi Sad. But I think that Simo talked to me and the journalist. I think that the recording will show what actually took place. I simply can't remember now. Or he took part in the preparation of the interview and then I thought it was Simo who carried out the interview. You see, I just don't know. MR. DI FAZIO: Would you fast-forward again, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A number of documents have come up on the screen, some showing typewritten lists, the one that we see before us now a handwritten list. Were you shown any such lists or given any such lists to comment on during the interview?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
