utterances.text: I don't know now whether this was shown to me while the interview was being prepared. There were some papers. I don't know if it was this precisely or something else. I'm not sure. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Please fast-forward.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Please stop there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is that gentleman? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is precisely the person I mentioned a while ago, Nizan Ramusovic, nicknamed Tota.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think you mentioned earlier in your evidence - and I'm sure Defence counsel will correct me if I'm wrong in this - but some days ago you mentioned in your evidence an episode between the members of the 4th Detachment and police in which there was a shoot-out of some sort and some people were wounded. Is this man that we see on the screen one of the men who was wounded, or can't you say?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was wounded in that shoot-out. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Please fast-forward.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Stop -- could we go back to that depiction of a photograph.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise that photograph at all? Have you got any idea who that person might be?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This person, as it says here, is Esad Visnjic. He was detained together with me over there at the MUP. I know that he said that he was on a train and when the bridge went down he happened to be at the railway station; and that's why they arrested him, simply because of his name. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Could we just continue into the next scene.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Could we stop there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to tell the Chamber, if you can, Mr. Tihic, if the ribbon on the shoulder -- whether you had seen it like that on previous occasions, just apparently hooked through an epaulette on the shoulder and just hanging down loosely. Is that the manner in which you had seen it previously?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That day when I saw Simo at the SUP, that's when I saw this, the first day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. MR. DI FAZIO: Fast-forward again, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is that man?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Omer Nalic, a prisoner who was with me. He came from Brcko. He wore glasses. He had bruises, I know, underneath, so he put glasses on so that it couldn't be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I take it he didn't have sunglasses in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He couldn't have. They did not -- they did not allow things like that to be kept in camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the clothes he's wearing? Was that what he was wearing in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Omer also changed at his house, or rather, his apartment. I'm not sure. I think he changed, of course. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Could we please fast-forward again?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Stop there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is the gentleman in the camouflage uniform, with the white hair?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the left-hand side is Simo. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Stop there, please. In fact, could we just scroll or rewind to the point where you can see the writing on the screen? Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's the writing on the screen say?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "Safet Hadzialijagic, nicknamed Coner, member of the military staff of the SDA for Bosanski Samac."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that in fact Safet Hadzialijagic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hadzialijagic, yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think anyone will object if I suggest that's you. Can you tell us what the writing on the screen says?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "Sulejman Tihic, lawyer, President of the SDA for Bosanski Samac, and member of the administration board of the SDA." MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Could we just pause it, please? Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Maybe I'm not so sure about this particular term. Maybe it will be more appropriate to say "executive board of SDA," not "administrative." I mean, maybe it's an issue of the translation. Of course, I'm not a professional, just a suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Counsel will correct that with -- or will clear that with the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just referring to what we saw previously on the screen that you read out, was the writing a reference to an administrative board or an executive board?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it said here on TV was a mistake, saying "administrative board." It was supposed to say "main board of the SDA," that being the top -- the top body in the party. However, by no means is it executive board. It does not say "executive." "Executive" would be an executive, a government; whereas "administrative board" is also wrong. No way. But that's what it said on the television. MR. DI FAZIO: I'd just like to play a small portion of the -- of this interview at this stage, if Your Honours please. For the purposes of the interpreters and for Defence counsel, and for the purposes of the Chamber, I think you can pick it up on the document that we've given to you at - again, looking at the top of the page for the ERN number - at the page ending 640. I believe that's where it picks up this portion of the interview. So if the gentleman in the technical room could rewind the video to the point where Mr. Tihic is introduced and starts to speak, I'd just like to play it for a short period of time so that we can hear his voice and play it at normal speed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Defence counsel is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we haven't got the text in the original language at all, or rather, we cannot hear the soundtrack at all. There is no sound whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: It may mean changing channels. Can you just find out, Prosecution counsel, please? MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Well, I've got channel 4 pressed and the video evidence button pressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I understand the technical people are looking at it because it was previously not meant to be transmitted into the courtroom. MR. DI FAZIO: I see. I do apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: They will see what they can do so that we can get it. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, perhaps for my purposes, I don't necessarily have to actually have any sound. I just wanted to provide the Chamber with an opportunity of just a better look at the face of Mr. Tihic because I want to ask him some questions about his appearance. So if we could just have a few more brief moments of normal transmission of the videotape at normal speed, even without sound, so we can all see Mr. Tihic's face? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Can I ask for the tape to be paused there? My purposes have essentially been achieved now, and I'll be fast-forwarding from this point onwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because the technical booth says that the volume was so low, the recorded volume was so low, that it's difficult to pick it up. I'm sure Defence counsel noticed that. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, I can proceed without it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. MR. DI FAZIO: But if we could have the video back, please, such that Mr. Tihic's face is depicted on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Tihic, you've had an opportunity of seeing yourself depicted. Firstly, the clothes that you're wearing, are they the clothes that you put on when you were taken to be cleaned up?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are clean clothes that I put on at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, look at your face. You have given evidence to the Chamber that you were beaten, and severely beaten, on numerous occasions in the -- both the TO building in Bosanski Samac and the police station in Bosanski Samac, although you've given evidence that you weren't beaten whilst in Brcko. It is not apparent, to me at least, that you have any wounds or anything like that on your face. Can you reconcile that apparent absence with the evidence that you've given?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what? I was hit a lot with a truncheon on my head, and my lips were cut and also my teeth were partially broken, so I have crowns now. But you know what it means when somebody is not beaten four days? The organism recovers amazingly. If anybody made me sign a statement that I would be beaten every third day and not beaten in the meantime, I would have signed it because it's amazing the extent to which you can recover. In Brcko, nobody beat us, as I told you, and my face recovered in some way. However, you'd have to see a bit of yellow here on the side, because when a bruise heals, you can see a yellowish hue because first a bruise is black or blue and then, as it fades, it turns yellow. And if the quality of the picture were better, I think it could be seen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now like you to keep looking carefully at the screen as we fast-forward further. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, please, if we could fast-forward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Can we stop there, please?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have just seen depiction of weapons and ammunition and bombs and so on. Were they in the interview room?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, they weren't. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Can we continue?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Can we just pause there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in the screen, we can see the apparent interviewer, yourself. Was there anyone else in the room at about that time?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Looking at the image, Simo was on my right side, and behind the journalist was Stevan Todorovic. So Simo Zaric was there, and Stevan Todorovic, and of course the camera operator.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, presumably you were asked questions and you gave your answers. Were the answers given of your own free will?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, the journalist asked us whether we wanted to give a statement. We said, in view of the circumstances we are in, yes, we said, we did want to. But really we were forced to be there. We were brought there against our will. And when I heard that we needed to go to Samac from Brcko, I felt sick because I knew what could await me there. So it wasn't because we wanted to be there of our own free will; we simply had to. What would have happened if I had said I didn't want to? I could have been beaten, and God knows what else could have happened. Crni was there, Stevan Todorovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the actual content of what you said? Were those freely spoken words?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That statement, I tried to speak in such a way so as to satisfy the people who were questioning us so that we wouldn't make them angry and at the same time, as much as possible, not to say things which were contrary to my convictions. I had to say that the Serb police did not beat us, which is not true, and other things also. You're in detention, so that does not really represent your own free will; so that the things that you are saying, you have to adapt to the ears of those who are interrogating you, and they happen to be the same people who also arrested you. So it wasn't really an expression of my real thoughts, but I tried to say something so that I wouldn't humiliate myself completely and that I wouldn't say anything at all but that it is sufficient for the people who were asking the questions for them to be satisfied and so as to avoid even worse consequences after the interview, to avoid being beaten even more. I was aware that if I had said something else, especially what I really thought about the treatment in the camps, that that is something that the television wouldn't even use. So I believed it was unnecessary to expose myself to such a risk. I would say something and I would be beaten because of it, or God knows what else, and they wouldn't end up broadcasting it anyway. You can see this coffee. They placed it in front of us, but nobody really sipped it. It looked as if I were drinking the coffee, but it just happened that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you were keen to avoid incurring any wrath or anger. Did you make any -- did anyone -- sorry, did any of the people present actually get angry with you at anything that you had said?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as far as I know. They did not. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Can we please continue by fast forwarding.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Just pausing there and going back further to show the buildings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What's that building that we saw with the spire?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the mosque, the mosque in Bosanski Samac. And a moment ago you could see the Catholic church. MR. DI FAZIO: Can we just rewind the tape.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Orthodox church. This is the Orthodox church.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think you can actually see any Catholic church there, can you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you rewind it a little more -- MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Could we do that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- you could see it. I saw it a moment ago on this side. Yes, there it is. That's the Catholic church. Opposite from the Orthodox church was the Catholic church. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Can we please fast-forward.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Can we stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, another feature that is apparent from looking at the video even when it's fast-forwarded is that you are gesticulating with your hands and apparently participating in the -- well, gesticulating with your hands. Was there any reason for that?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a habit of gesticulating with my hands when I'm speaking, and that's what you can see here. This is just the way I am. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Stop there, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you recognise the gentleman in the dark glasses?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is Izet Izetbegovic. He was also full of bruises. And he's wearing glasses, but I think those are his glasses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the man in front of him? Is that an interviewer?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Can we please fast-forward.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Can we just rewind that tape to the portion where some writing appears on the screen of this gentleman's interview. Right. Just that piece of writing that we can see there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What does that say, Mr. Tihic?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "Izet Izetbegovic, member of the Main Committee of the SDA." But let's correct it. Once again, Izet Izetbegovic was not a member of the Main Committee; he was the vice-president of the SDA for Bosanski Samac, where I was the president. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Can we continue, please.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. Has the video been given an exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I think it was P16, and then the English P16A, and the B/C/S P16A ter. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I'm grateful to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Obviously you've seen it now, but were you shown the programme or the interview in which you participated at all in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you shown it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I had the tape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you get it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was recorded by an acquaintance of mine, Ivo Kobas, and he gave it to me sometime later, in 1995, because it was shown on TV Novi Sad and he recorded it, and then he made a copy and he gave it to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do with the copy? Did you ever give it to anyone, the copy that you got?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's at home in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's return to the day of the actual interview itself. Did you see the interview or tape of the interview on the day that you participated in it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken back to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When after the interview? That day? Days later?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day I know they were in a hurry because they didn't want the members of the special forces to appear, so it was all very, very speedy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you taken back to the Brcko barracks?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was taken back to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Imprisoned again?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you remain at Brcko from that point onwards?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe another two days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any shelling or bombing in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard a powerful detonation one morning which caused the windows to shatter on the prison building, and it was so powerful that the metal door opened and the guards started shouting, "Wait." Probably they were thinking we were going to try to escape, but we didn't. And then we heard shooting. They were bringing some people there, beating them. Then sometime in the afternoon, at about 1.00 or 2.00 p.m., the captain who was in charge of the prison called Lukac and myself and told us that we should all get ready and that they would transfer us to Bijeljina, because war had broken out in Brcko, and that was the reason why we were being transferred. A bus stopped in front. We went into the bus. I know that one person who was being beaten, who had been beaten, was with us, and they just put him into the bus. But he wasn't all there. He didn't seem normal. Then on the road from Brcko to Bijeljina, we came to the barracks in Bijeljina. The barracks was called Fadil Jahic Spanac. And then that person who was from Brcko -- I didn't see it, but the others told me that as soon as he came out of the bus, they shot him. And they took us first upstairs and then later they took us to the gymnasium. And there, there was a sort of combination. They both beat us, even though there were officers there during whose shift they didn't permit anybody to beat us. But there was also a person who hit me several times. He saw me wearing my suit, and I looked like a gentleman to him, so he said, "What are you doing here?" So that every time that he was on the shift, he would hit me with his truncheon. I was also beaten badly once in Bijeljina, when they took me to clean the toilets. It's a squatting toilet, and it was very soiled, and I had to clean that with my hands. He beat me. I fell, and I had to clean everything up and make that horrible yellow mess white. And they beat me for a hour or two until they called me to go back to that area where the other inmates were. And when I went inside that room, I could see five people with -- whose eyes were bound, and they told me to stand there and they also bound my eyes. And they -- they blindfolded me, and then soon they took us out of that room. We didn't know where we were going. And I could hear the sound of the helicopter. They brought -- they put us into the helicopter. There was a coffin there with a cross on the lid of that coffin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to pause there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Izet Izetbegovic was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, where is Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bijeljina is in Bosnia, and it's close to the border with Serbia. I can show it on the map for you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please just indicate for the Chamber on the Times map of the Balkans.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So it appears to be on the border with Serbia?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The barracks that you've described, were there military men guarding you and apparently walking around?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was a barracks of the JNA, and there were military officers there. There were regular members of the army. There were also reserve forces, officers. There was even a Muslim among them, a person called Saban, and when he was working, he wouldn't allow them to beat us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've referred to soldiers called "specials." Were there any such "specials" at Bijeljina, the barracks in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There weren't any when we were there. There was a person there who threatened us by saying, "Well, Arkan's men will come back and then you will see," but they weren't there when we were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how long did you remain in Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we spent one or two nights there, two nights, and then we were transferred by helicopter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: About how many prisoners were there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our whole group from Tuzla. We were all transferred to Bijeljina. But only several of us were separated and placed in the helicopter, while the others remained in the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Bosanski Samac people? How many Bosanski Samac people were in custody there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe there were about 50 people from Samac, but the people who were taken into the helicopter were the so-called political inmates, that group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that -- what makes you say that those selected to go in the helicopter were political inmates?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those people were -- were the people that Simo called political inmates at the barracks in Brcko. Dragan Lukac was there. He was the chief of police. Anto Simovic was the director of the veterinary station. Sejo Mujkanovic, he was a regular policeman. I was a lawyer, President of the SDA. [redacted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you were there for a couple of days possibly and eventually --

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Franjo Barukcic. He was the director of the steel works.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you were present there for two nights and then you were taken away by helicopter. Just tell us where you were taken to by helicopter, and then I'll ask you some questions about the trip.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They took us -- later on we found out that it was Batajnica, a military airport near Belgrade in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Just point out on the map where Batajnica is so that the Chamber can see where this location is.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [indicates]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I just approach the map? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Batajnica is a little bit above Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the trip itself in the helicopter, was it an army helicopter?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was a military helicopter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many prisoners in it?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Besides us, the people I mentioned, we found three other people there: Izet Izetbegovic, Dr. Miroslav Feracic, and Anto Dragicevic, all from Bosanski Samac. He was the father of the former chief of police, Mitar. Also in the chopper were also some of Arkan's men, and they were wearing a certain type of cap. There was also a civilian. And later, in Batajnica, I found out that he was in charge of security. He was a major and he was in charge of security affairs. And in the middle, there was that coffin with the cross on it. And I think the name of that person who was in the coffin was Vuk, Vuk Mirovic, something like that. The person in the cap kept wanting to throw us outside, but the person in civilian clothes, the person I found out later was in charge of security affairs, whom I got to know later in Batajnica, said, "No, no, not now. We will do it later." We all were handcuffed with steel handcuffs, so it would be enough to push one person for all of us to go down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thanks. Just tell us how long you remained in Batajnica and where you were next taken. I just want to know the period of time in Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Batajnica from the 3rd to the 27th of May. There was a lot of beating and mistreatment there also, all kinds of things. After that, we were transferred, some of us. Izet Izetbegovic, I think it was his birthday on the 25th, and that's when he was transferred to Pale for exchange. Dragan Lukac, [redacted], and Franjo Barukcic and another person were taken to Bosnia. Fadil Topcagic came to get them -- and, I don't know, another policeman. And then the next day, the rest of us were transferred on the 27th to the military camp at Sremska Mitrovica, and this was in Serbia, i.e., in Voyvodina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm interested in the episode where Fadil Topcagic came to get some of the prisoners. Can you recall at what point of your time at Batajnica he turned up?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fadil appeared on the 26th, and that's when he took them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you speak to him?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did speak. I know that he brought us apples, he shared out apples amongst us. He said, "These people were going for an exchange." And I asked him, "What about me?" And he said he was going to come back later for me and the others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he apparently lead away or take away the prisoners for exchange?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was there, and there was another person from Obudovac. I can't remember the name of that young man, because also, when we went to the TV station in Samac, he was also accompanying Fadil. Of course, there was also the warrant officer who was there at the barracks in Batajnica. He was a kind of chief of the shifts and he was present when Fadil took those people away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he provide you with any details as to when he would come back later for you?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He said he was going to come back in two or three days, but the next day we were transferred to Mitrovica, Sremska Mitrovica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to the conditions that you experienced at Batajnica. I don't want to go through each and every episode that happened there, but can you just generally tell the Court the sorts of -- the sort of treatment that was meted out to you there?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in a cellar which had small windows just above the ground level, but those windows were covered with green blankets so that there was no daylight in those rooms. There was one lamp which was burning. It was a room with a low ceiling, with cement on the floor. And they gave us mattresses, one by one. They were sponge mattresses. And there was torture, abuse, beating, singing of songs. The shifts changed every three hours. Somebody would come at midnight, then another shift at 3.00 a.m. Whoever would come, they would request for us to sing songs or jump around. There was -- we were being beaten a lot there. I was surprised when I came to Batajnica, there was a picture of Draza Mihajlovic. And in the morning when we got up -- somebody had drawn that picture on the wall. When we got up, when -- we would have to kiss that picture and say, "Good morning, General," and then we would continue with our business, go to the toilet. Later, I found out that this was at some kind of -- that this was some kind of medical facility, medical centre, and we were in the basement. Sometimes when they would beat us, they would bring a doctor. There was a doctor there, a woman doctor, who had lived in Zadar, so she would talk to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did she treat you, treat you medically?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. She would give us different medication for pain or if some wounds needed to be dressed or she would put ointment on them and so on. Some people would come and beat us. Then the next shift would come and they would bring a doctor and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the songs? What sort of songs were you forced to sing?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would sing all the Chetnik songs, and they made me and Izet Izetbegovic sing a song about Alija Izetbegovic, and it was a song that went more like this: "At the top of the Romanija mountain, Alija's skin is flying around in the wind. We will make casings for our weapons out of it." And so that then everybody who was there had to join in the singing of that song. Then there were also a song by Tajci, "Let's go crazy this night. Let's gouge out the eyes of Croats." This is something that the Croats had to sing. There was another one. There was a Muslim woman who swore in front of a mosque that she -- the man she loved the most was a Serb. So all of these were the kinds of songs that they would ask us to sing. Also the song, "From Topola to Ravna Gora." So these were the songs that we had to sing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned having to jump around. I don't think that conveys to the Chamber precisely what was involved. Could you please give -- provide them with some detail of what exactly that did involve?

utterances.speaker: SULEJMAN TIHIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called it a sort of mole jump, from the mole. We had to crouch down and then jump up. They would place chairs two metres away from one another, and then we would have to go around those chairs. For example, they would give you five seconds that you would -- had to crawl around one chair, the second chair, the third chair, go to the corridor, pour in a pitcher of water and then come back, and the person would be counting, "One, two," and you would be hurrying, hurrying. And then when he would get close to four, he would say, "Four, five," quickly and so on, until they got tired of it. And then they would allow you to actually take the five seconds in order to pass all of those obstacles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you personally --

utterances.text: Counsel, it's 1.00. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm sorry, I wasn't following the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We are starting at 14.15. MR. DI FAZIO: I think that the end of my examination-in-chief is in sight now. And I can indicate that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: About how many more minutes tomorrow? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I can't predict entirely with any great certainty. There is just one more videotape that I want to introduce, but certainly tomorrow I'm hopeful that my examination-in-chief will conclude.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Tomorrow we will sit at 14.15 hours and take a break and resume at 15.45 hours. And I wanted to find out from the Defence counsel whether, for Mr. Simic, for instance, whether it is -- we can sit up to 1900 hours?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, since I don't speak the language, my colleague over here will translate. He spoke to my client and found out what was appropriate for him tomorrow. So I'll let him speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have talked to Mr. Simic with regard to both possibilities, and he said to me that if the trial were to begin at 2.15 and end at 7.00 p.m. it would be virtually impossible for him to sit in the courtroom for four hours and to have a 45-minute break. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. In that case, then, we will sit 14.15 and take a break, and then resume at 15.45 -- no, no, sit at 14.15 until 15.45, take a half-hour break and then sit again at 16.15 until 17.45. That's acceptable. Okay. Those are the hours for tomorrow. The Court will rise.
